meta.title: Who really said "Wherefore art thou, Romeo?" | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare wrote it, but not that way. Juliet's line is "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" — and wherefore means why, not where.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wherefore art thou, Romeo?'
meta.ogDescription: Juliet never says "Wherefore art thou, Romeo?" The 1599 quarto reads "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" — wherefore means why.

answer.label: Shakespeare — but misquoted
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely Shakespeare’s — Juliet speaks it in Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2, the balcony scene. But what he wrote is longer and pointed differently: “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” No early printing shortens it to “Wherefore art thou, Romeo?”, and none puts a comma before that last name. That added comma is what turns Juliet’s question — why must you be a Romeo? — into the modern misreading where are you?

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Act 2, Scene 2 — the balcony scene (line 33 in the 1865 Cambridge text)
Juliet, believing herself alone; Romeo is listening unseen below
1597 (Q1, London); 1599 (Q2), the copy-text modern editions follow

source.excerpt:
JULIET: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo?
Deny thy father and refuse thy name;
Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,
And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
ROMEO (aside): Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
trail: The line is Juliet’s in Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2, at the Folger Shakespeare Library ↗, where it is printed “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

The earliest text modern editors follow prints it the same way: the Internet Shakespeare Editions transcription of the 1599 second quarto ↗ reads “Iuli. O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo? / Denie thy father and refuse thy name” — with no comma before the final name.

Folger’s editors explain the choice of copy-text: “Recent editors have been virtually unanimous in their selection of the Second Quarto as the basis for their editions” ↗ — the 1599 printing, not the shorter 1597 one.

The misreading is a vocabulary problem as much as a punctuation one: the Phrase Finder notes the line “would appear to be” asking ‘Where are you Romeo?’ ↗, then corrects it — “wherefore” means why, not where.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text: the three lines after the famous one are as Wikiquote transcribes them from the 1865 Cambridge edition of Clark and Wright, and the MIT complete works prints the famous line with an exclamation mark. The 1599 quarto has a comma there instead — “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” In none of them is there a comma before the final “Romeo.”

source.rightsNote: Romeo and Juliet was first printed in London in 1597 and again, “newly corrected, augmented, and amended,” in 1599 — so the play and this line are firmly in the public domain in the United States. The modern-spelling wording quoted above follows nineteenth-century editions (Clark and Wright’s 1865 Cambridge text, itself public domain); only a particular modern editor’s text, notes or apparatus could carry rights of its own.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare was, in Wikipedia’s summary, “an English playwright, poet and actor.” Romeo and Juliet reached print twice in his lifetime in sharply different forms — a short 1597 quarto and a fuller 1599 one advertised as “newly corrected, augmented, and amended” — and it is the 1599 text that editors follow today. The balcony speech turns entirely on one archaic word: in Shakespeare’s English wherefore means why, so Juliet is interrogating Romeo’s name, not his whereabouts.

copyAttribution: Misquote of William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, Scene 2. As printed in the 1599 second quarto the line runs “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” — there is no comma before the final name, because “wherefore” means “why,” not “where.”

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: The author credit is correct — this is one of the rare famous lines that really does come from the play it is pinned to. What has drifted is the wording, and with it the meaning.

items.why: Shakespeare’s line opens with the doubled name and does not stop where the popular version does: the 1599 second quarto reads “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” ↗. The clipped five-word form appears in no early printing of the play.

In the early text the last “Romeo” is what Juliet is asking about, not someone she is calling to — the 1599 quarto prints “wherefore art thou Romeo?” with no comma before the name ↗. Adding one makes it an address, which is exactly what invites the ‘where are you’ reading.

“Wherefore” means why. As Oliver Tearle puts it, “she isn’t, of course, asking him where he is” ↗ — Juliet has just learned the boy she loves is a Montague, and she is asking why he has to bear that name.

Even the early texts differ at the front of the line: the 1597 first quarto opens the speech “Ah Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” ↗, not “O.” What does not differ is the absence of a comma before the final name.

misattribution.truthLine: What Shakespeare actually wrote — and what Wikiquote transcribes at Act II, scene ii, line 33 ↗ — is “O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? / Deny thy father and refuse thy name.” Juliet’s very next line answers the question she just asked, which no request for directions would need.

context.heading: A question, not a search party
lead: Juliet is on her balcony, believing herself alone, having just discovered that the boy she fell for at her family’s party is a Montague. Romeo is in fact below, listening unheard. Her line is a complaint about a name: why must you be a Romeo? The proof is the line immediately after it — “Deny thy father and refuse thy name” — which answers a ‘why,’ not a ‘where.’

The popular version does two small things with large consequences: it drops the doubled “O Romeo, Romeo,” and it slips a comma in before the last name. That comma converts “Romeo” from the thing being questioned into a person being hailed, and the whole speech is quietly rewritten as a girl calling into the dark for a missing boyfriend — the reading the Phrase Finder flags as what the line only appears to mean.
detailsBody: Romeo and Juliet survives in two markedly different early quartos. The 1597 Q1 — “An excellent conceited tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet”, printed in London by Edward Allde and John Danter — gives Juliet’s speech as “Ah Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”

The 1599 Q2 — “The most excellent and lamentable tragedie, of Romeo and Iuliet. Newly corrected, augmented, and amended”, printed by Thomas Creede for Cuthbert Burby — has “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” That is the reading modern editions inherit, because Q2 is the copy-text they are, in Folger’s words, “virtually unanimous” in choosing.
The two can be read side by side in P. A. Daniel’s parallel-text edition of the first two quartos, published for the New Shakspere Society in 1874 and scanned at the Internet Archive.
context.pull: Juliet is not asking where Romeo is. She is asking why he has to be a Romeo at all.
